artwork.title: The Virgin of the Rocks
artwork.imageCredit: Reproduction via Wikimedia Commons (from gallerix.ru) · Public Domain
artwork.medium: Oil on canvas, transferred from wood

lessons.title: One contract, two paintings

n1.text: Step into a cave. Rocks close in on every side and plants sprout from the stone. In a pool of light, four figures: Mary at the centre, a baby on each side of her, an angel on the right.

voice.speaker: leonardo
voice.text: Look before you ask. Who kneels? Who blesses? Where does each hand point? In a picture, the gestures tell the story.

q1.text: Where did your eye land first?

b1a.text: Good eye. The angel turns to look out at you while its finger points across the group. Hold on to that angel: Leonardo changed its pose.

b1b.text: Few people start there. Mary's left hand floats above the baby on the right, fingers spread. Keep it in mind; it's one of the picture's quiet gestures.

b1c.text: The rocks hem everyone in, and light picks the figures out against the dark stone. Modelling forms with light and dark like this is called chiaroscuro.

n2.text: So who's who? Mary kneels at the centre, her arm round the kneeling baby on the left: John the Baptist. The baby on the right, steadied by the angel, is Jesus, raising his hand to bless John.

n2b.text: This was ordered as an altarpiece. On 25 April 1483, in Milan, Leonardo signed a contract with two local painters, the brothers Ambrogio and Evangelista de Predis, for a chapel in the church of San Francesco Grande.

voice.speaker: leonardo
voice.text: Milan, 1483. I signed with the de Predis brothers: a painting for a chapel at San Francesco Grande.

q2.text: The chapel belonged to a confraternity. What was it devoted to?

b2a.text: Yes. The Immaculate Conception means Mary was conceived without the stain of original sin. The painting sat at the heart of a big carved and gilded altarpiece made for that chapel.

b2b.text: Good instinct: that's what you see. But it isn't what the chapel was devoted to.

correction.tempting: Everyone in the picture kneels before the child Jesus, so it looks like a straightforward Adoration.
correction.truth: The scene is an adoration, but the confraternity that ordered it was devoted to the Immaculate Conception: Mary conceived without original sin.
correction.evidence: The Louvre and London's National Gallery both name the client: the Confraternity of the Immaculate Conception at San Francesco Grande, Milan.

b2c.text: Fair guess: John is right there, and the angel points at him. But no.

correction.tempting: John kneels in the front of the picture and the angel's finger points at him, so he looks like the star.
correction.truth: John matters in this painting, but the confraternity that ordered it was devoted to the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin.
correction.evidence: The Louvre and the National Gallery both name the Confraternity of the Immaculate Conception as the client for the chapel.

n3.text: Then came trouble. Leonardo and Ambrogio said the agreed fee was too low for the work, and asked the confraternity for more money.

n3b.text: The quarrel dragged on for more than twenty years. Along the way Leonardo probably sold this first picture, and a second version was painted for the chapel. That one hangs in London's National Gallery today.

voice.speaker: leonardo
voice.text: We asked for more money, and the quarrel outlived my first years in Milan. They called me back in 1506 to finish.

q3.text: So why are there two Virgins of the Rocks?

choices.label: The first didn't suit the altarpiece

b3a.text: The quarrel is real, but it doesn't explain the second picture.

correction.tempting: A fight over pay lasting more than twenty years looks like the obvious cause of everything that followed.
correction.truth: The quarrel is documented, but no source says it caused the second version. Historians have offered conflicting explanations.
correction.evidence: The National Gallery: "It is not clear why two versions were made." The Louvre: historians have given "explications contradictoires".

b3b.text: That's one serious argument, not a settled fact.

correction.tempting: In London the figures are bigger and closer, as if built to hold their own inside a heavy carved frame.
correction.truth: That's an argument the National Gallery puts forward, not a proven reason. Neither museum claims to know why two versions exist.
correction.evidence: The National Gallery says the London figures "appear bigger and closer", yet also that "It is not clear why two versions were made."

b3c.text: Right. The National Gallery says plainly it isn't clear why two versions were made, and the Louvre says historians give conflicting explanations. Each idea has some evidence; none settles it.

n4.text: What both museums agree on: this Paris picture came first. Even its dates differ, though: about 1483 to 1494 for the Louvre, about 1483 to 1485 for the National Gallery. And who painted most of London is still argued.

n4b.text: Now compare the angels. In London, the angel looks down into the group and steadies Jesus; it doesn't point. Here, the angel turns to look at you and points across at John.

q4.text: Was this pointing, outward-looking angel Leonardo's first idea?

b4a.text: It looks planned, but no: the pose was a change of mind.

correction.tempting: The gesture is so natural, and links you to the scene so neatly, that it seems designed from day one.
correction.truth: Leonardo altered the angel's pose from his first plan. The figure that looks out and points was not there from the start.
correction.evidence: The Louvre and the Grand Palais's art-history site, Panorama de l'art, both say Leonardo modified the angel's attitude from his initial design.

b4b.text: Right. Leonardo altered this angel's pose from his first plan. As painted, it looks out of the picture at you and points across to John.

n5.text: So the final angel is your guide into the scene: its eyes find you, and its finger points you to John.

voice.speaker: leonardo
voice.text: Follow a figure's eyes, then its hand. That's how a painting tells you where to look.

q5.text: The label says oil on canvas. Did Leonardo paint it on canvas?

choices.label: No: wood, moved to canvas later
Yes, on canvas from the start

b5a.text: Right. Leonardo painted it on a wooden panel. Later it was transferred from wood to canvas, which is why the Louvre records it as oil on canvas today.

b5b.text: Read the label to the end: there's a second half.

correction.tempting: The Louvre's own label starts with "oil on canvas", so canvas from the start seems obvious.
correction.truth: The label goes on: transferred from wood to canvas. Leonardo painted on a wooden panel; the move to canvas came later.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: "Huile sur toile (transposition de bois sur toile)". The National Gallery's technical study: oil on wood, transferred to canvas.

n6.text: It later entered the French royal collection; exactly how is uncertain. So in room 710 you meet the first of a famous pair: a cave of light and shade, and an angel Leonardo rethought to point you in.

lessons.takeaway: Paris has the first Virgin of the Rocks: light picking four figures out of a dark cave, an angel Leonardo rethought to point you to John, and a twin in London.
